title: Explicit Phonics Instruction in the Context of Reading Workshop
author: Dr. Andy Johnson
summary: In this chapter excerpt, the second in a three-part series on reading workshop, Johnson argues that reading workshop includes direct, explicit and systematic phonics instruction, contrary to common mischaracterisation. He distinguishes what he calls intelligent phonics instruction from unintelligent phonics instruction, the latter marked by rigid scripts and isolated sounds. He holds that systematic phonics should provide structure without rigid control, sitting between chaos and control on a continuum. He cites research questioning whether rigid systematic phonics outperforms other approaches and whether skills transfer to authentic reading. A wrestling-coach analogy illustrates the case for brief targeted instruction embedded in plenty of authentic practice.
points: Reading workshop is often mischaracterised as excluding phonics, yet direct and explicit instruction is an essential part of it.
He contrasts intelligent phonics, which is targeted, brief and embedded in authentic reading, with unintelligent phonics, which is scripted and isolated.
Systematic phonics should follow a general plan, providing structure without being structured, between the extremes of chaos and control.
He claims that evidence is insufficient to show rigid systematic phonics is more effective than balanced approaches or whole language.
The wrestling analogy shows that drilling skills without authentic practice yields little transfer from practice room to match.
quotes: Reading workshop is often mischaracterized as excluding direct and explicit phonics instruction. This is simply not true. Direct and explicit instruction of phonics and other skills is an essential part of reading workshop.
Educational publishers are strongly in favor of unintelligent phonics instruction. This is the kind of phonics instruction that sells products.
Systematic phonics instruction means that it takes place according to a fixed plan. What’s at issue here is what that plan is and how fixed it should be.

A more appropriate understanding of systematic phonics instruction is used with reading workshop. It includes a general plan for teaching a more basic set of letter sounds and patterns. These are taught as students are ready for them and as they are encountered in print.
Systematic phonics instruction is found on a continuum with chaos on one end and control on the other (see Figure 2). Both ends of the continuum are suboptimal for reading achievement.

While research has shown that phonics-based instruction can lead to increased scores on phonics-based measures (Allor, Mathes, Roberts, Cheatham, & Al Otaiba, 2014; Browder, Ahlgrim-Delzell, Flowers, & Baker, 2012; Hill, 2016); there is little transfer of these skills to authentic reading conditions (Pearson & Heibert, 2013).

if I spent most of wrestling practice teaching skills and drilling, my wrestlers might know a lot of skills in the short term, but they wouldn’t know how and when to apply them in authentic wrestling conditions. There’d be little transfer between the practice room and the match.
